solution:
Both A and B are volatile, so Raoult's law applies to each component of the liquid mixture, \(p_A = p_A^\circ x_A\) and \(p_B = p_B^\circ x_B\), and by Dalton's law of partial pressures \(p_{\text{total}} = p_A + p_B\).
Putting \(x_B = 1 - x_A\):
\(p_{\text{total}} = p_A^\circ x_A + p_B^\circ (1 - x_A) = p_B^\circ + (p_A^\circ - p_B^\circ) x_A\)
\(600 = 700 + (450 - 700) x_A = 700 - 250 x_A\)
so \(x_A = 100/250 = 0.40\) and \(x_B = 0.60\).
The partial pressures are then \(p_A = 450 \times 0.40 = 180\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(p_B = 700 \times 0.60 = 420\,\text{mm Hg}\) (check: \(180 + 420 = 600\,\text{mm Hg}\)).
The vapour-phase composition is NOT these liquid-phase values. It follows from Dalton's law, \(y_i = p_i / p_{\text{total}}\):
\(y_A = 180/600 = 0.30\), \(y_B = 420/600 = 0.70\).
Liquid phase: \(x_A = 0.40\), \(x_B = 0.60\). Vapour phase: \(y_A = 0.30\), \(y_B = 0.70\) — the vapour is richer in B, the more volatile component.

In pure ethanol the molecules are held to one another by hydrogen bonds between alcohol molecules, and in pure water by hydrogen bonds between water molecules. On mixing, water molecules get in between the alcohol molecules and break some of those alcohol-alcohol hydrogen bonds, and the alcohol-water hydrogen bonds formed in their place are weaker than the average of the original alcohol-alcohol and water-water interactions. Calling alcohol A and water B, the A-B interaction is weaker than the A-A and B-B interactions.
Because each kind of molecule is now held less tightly than it was in its own pure liquid, its escaping tendency into the vapour increases, so \(p_A > p_A^\circ x_A\) and \(p_B > p_B^\circ x_B\) and the total vapour pressure lies above the value Raoult's law predicts.
Hence the molecular interactions make an alcohol-water solution a non-ideal one showing POSITIVE deviation from Raoult's law. Since the energy needed to break the stronger A-A and B-B hydrogen bonds exceeds that released in forming the weaker A-B ones, mixing is endothermic, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H > 0\), and the looser packing gives \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V > 0\). It is this positive deviation that gives ethanol and water their minimum-boiling azeotrope.

An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole composition range, \(p_A = p_A^\circ x_A\) and \(p_B = p_B^\circ x_B\), so each partial pressure and the total pressure plot as straight lines against mole fraction. A deviation is a departure of the measured pressure from those straight lines.
Positive deviation: \(p_A > p_A^\circ x_A\) and \(p_B > p_B^\circ x_B\), so the measured \(p_{\text{total}}\) lies ABOVE the Raoult's law line. The cause is that the A-B interaction is WEAKER than the A-A and B-B interactions, so each molecule is held less tightly than in its pure liquid and escapes more readily. Breaking the stronger A-A and B-B contacts costs more energy than is released in forming the weaker A-B contacts, so mixing absorbs heat. Examples: ethanol and water, acetone and carbon disulphide, ethanol and acetone.
Negative deviation: \(p_A < p_A^\circ x_A\) and \(p_B < p_B^\circ x_B\), so the measured \(p_{\text{total}}\) lies BELOW the Raoult's law line. The cause is that the A-B interaction is STRONGER than the A-A and B-B interactions — often a new hydrogen bond between the unlike molecules — so each component is held more tightly than in its pure liquid and its escaping tendency falls. The energy released in forming the stronger A-B contacts exceeds that needed to break A-A and B-B, so mixing gives out heat. Examples: chloroform and acetone, nitric acid and water, phenol and aniline.
Relation to the enthalpy of mixing: a positive deviation goes with an endothermic mixing, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H > 0\) (and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V > 0\)); a negative deviation goes with an exothermic mixing, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H < 0\) (and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V < 0\)); for an ideal solution there is no deviation and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H = 0\).

Both components are volatile and the solution is ideal, so Raoult's law holds for each and, by Dalton's law, \(p_{\text{total}} = p^\circ_{\text{hep}} x_{\text{hep}} + p^\circ_{\text{oct}} x_{\text{oct}}\), where the mole fractions are those of the LIQUID phase.
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: heptane \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}\), \(M = 7(12) + 16(1) = 100\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); octane \(\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}\), \(M = 8(12) + 18(1) = 114\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{hep}} = 26.0/100 = 0.260\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{oct}} = 35/114 = 0.307\,\text{mol}\), total \(= 0.567\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_{\text{hep}} = 0.260/0.567 = 0.4585\), \(x_{\text{oct}} = 1 - 0.4585 = 0.5415\).
\(p_{\text{total}} = (105.2)(0.4585) + (46.8)(0.5415) = 48.24 + 25.34 = 73.58\,\text{kPa}\).
Vapour pressure of the mixture \(= 73.6\,\text{kPa}\).

The solute is non-volatile, so it contributes nothing to the vapour and Raoult's law reduces to \(p = p^\circ x_{\text{solvent}}\).
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of SOLVENT, so a 1 molal solution contains \(1\,\text{mol}\) of solute in \(1000\,\text{g}\) of water. With \(M(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 2(1) + 16 = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\),
\(n_{\text{water}} = 1000/18 = 55.56\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_{\text{water}} = \frac{55.56}{55.56 + 1} = \frac{55.56}{56.56} = 0.9823\).
\(p = (12.3)(0.9823) = 12.08\,\text{kPa}\).
Vapour pressure of the solution \(= 12.08\,\text{kPa}\), i.e. a lowering of about \(0.22\,\text{kPa}\).

For a non-volatile solute Raoult's law gives \(p = p^\circ x_{\text{solvent}}\), which rearranges to the relative lowering of vapour pressure being equal to the mole fraction of the solute, \(\frac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_{\text{solute}}\).
Reducing the vapour pressure to 80% means \(p = 0.80\,p^\circ\), so \(x_{\text{solvent}} = 0.80\) and \(x_{\text{solute}} = 0.20\).
Octane is \(\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}\), \(M = 8(12) + 18(1) = 114\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so \(114\,\text{g}\) of octane is exactly \(1.00\,\text{mol}\).
Let \(n\) be the moles of solute. Then \(\frac{n}{n + 1} = 0.20\), so \(n = 0.20n + 0.20\), giving \(0.80n = 0.20\) and \(n = 0.25\,\text{mol}\).
Mass \(= n \times M = (0.25)(40) = 10\,\text{g}\).
Mass of non-volatile solute required \(= 10\,\text{g}\).
_note: Read 'reduce its vapour pressure to 80%' as p = 0.80 p-degree (the standard reading, and the one the phrase 'to 80%' carries). Read instead as a reduction BY 80% it would give x_solute = 0.80 and a mass of 160 g.

solution:
Glucose is a non-volatile, non-electrolytic solute, so only water contributes to the vapour pressure and Raoult's law gives \(p = p^\circ x_{\text{water}}\).
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\), \(M = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); water \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(M = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{glucose}} = 25/180 = 0.1389\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{water}} = 450/18 = 25.0\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_{\text{water}} = \frac{25.0}{25.0 + 0.1389} = \frac{25.0}{25.1389} = 0.99448\).
\(p = (17.535)(0.99448) = 17.438\,\text{mm Hg}\).
Vapour pressure of the solution at \(293\,\text{K} = 17.44\,\text{mm Hg}\), a lowering of about \(0.097\,\text{mm Hg}\).

Both liquids are volatile, so by Raoult's law and Dalton's law \(p_{\text{total}} = p_A^\circ x_A + p_B^\circ x_B\), the mole fractions being those of the liquid phase.
\(n_A = 100/140 = 0.7143\,\text{mol}\), \(n_B = 1000/180 = 5.5556\,\text{mol}\), total \(= 6.2698\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_A = 0.7143/6.2698 = 0.1139\), \(x_B = 1 - 0.1139 = 0.8861\).
B alone contributes \(p_B = p_B^\circ x_B = (500)(0.8861) = 443.04\,\text{torr}\).
So the partial pressure of A in the solution is \(p_A = p_{\text{total}} - p_B = 475 - 443.04 = 31.96\,\text{torr}\).
And from Raoult's law for A, \(p_A^\circ = \frac{p_A}{x_A} = \frac{31.96}{0.1139} = 280.6\,\text{torr}\).
Vapour pressure of pure liquid A \(= 280.6\,\text{torr}\); vapour pressure (partial pressure) of A in the solution \(= 32.0\,\text{torr}\).

The straight lines to be drawn against \(x_{\text{acetone}}\) are the Raoult's law (ideal) ones:
\(p_{\text{acetone}} = 741.8\,x_{\text{acetone}}\), rising linearly from \(0\) to \(741.8\,\text{mm Hg}\);
\(p_{\text{chloroform}} = 632.8\,(1 - x_{\text{acetone}})\), falling linearly from \(632.8\) to \(0\,\text{mm Hg}\);
\(p_{\text{total}} = 632.8 + 109.0\,x_{\text{acetone}}\), rising linearly from \(632.8\) to \(741.8\,\text{mm Hg}\).
The experimental total pressure is the sum of the two measured partial pressures. Comparing it with the ideal line:

| \(x_{\text{acetone}}\) | 0 | 0.118 | 0.234 | 0.360 | 0.508 | 0.582 | 0.645 | 0.721 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| observed \(p_{\text{total}}\) /mm Hg | 632.8 | 603.0 | 579.5 | 562.1 | 580.4 | 599.5 | 615.3 | 641.8 |
| ideal \(p_{\text{total}}\) /mm Hg | 632.8 | 645.7 | 658.3 | 672.0 | 688.2 | 696.2 | 703.1 | 711.4 |

Every observed point lies below its ideal value, and so does each observed partial pressure taken separately. For instance at \(x_{\text{acetone}} = 0.508\) the measured \(p_{\text{acetone}} = 322.7\,\text{mm Hg}\) against an ideal \((741.8)(0.508) = 376.8\,\text{mm Hg}\), and the measured \(p_{\text{chloroform}} = 257.7\,\text{mm Hg}\) against an ideal \((632.8)(0.492) = 311.3\,\text{mm Hg}\). Plotted on the same axes, all three experimental curves sag below their straight ideal lines, and the experimental total pressure curve passes through a MINIMUM near \(x_{\text{acetone}} \approx 0.36\) that lies below the vapour pressure of either pure liquid.
That is the signature of a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law. The reason is that acetone and chloroform attract each other more strongly than either attracts its own kind: the C-H hydrogen of chloroform is made acidic by the three electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms and forms a hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen of acetone. This A-B interaction is stronger than the acetone-acetone dipole-dipole and chloroform-chloroform interactions, so the escaping tendency of both components is lowered and each partial pressure falls below \(p^\circ x\). Consistently, mixing is exothermic with \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H < 0\) and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V < 0\), and the minimum in the vapour-pressure curve corresponds to a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
The acetone-chloroform mixture shows NEGATIVE deviation from ideal behaviour.
_note: The row asks for a graph. No solution diagram is authored for this chapter, so the answer specifies the three ideal straight lines to draw, tabulates the observed total against the ideal total at every given composition (the comparison the plot is meant to make visible), and states the verdict with its molecular reason.

solution:
The solution is ideal, so Raoult's law gives the partial pressures from the LIQUID-phase mole fractions, and Dalton's law then gives the VAPOUR-phase mole fractions — the two are different numbers and it is the vapour one that is asked for.
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: benzene \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\), \(M = 6(12) + 6(1) = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); toluene \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\), \(M = 7(12) + 8(1) = 92\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{ben}} = 80/78 = 1.0256\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{tol}} = 100/92 = 1.0870\,\text{mol}\), total \(= 2.1126\,\text{mol}\).
Liquid phase: \(x_{\text{ben}} = 1.0256/2.1126 = 0.4855\), \(x_{\text{tol}} = 0.5145\).
Raoult's law: \(p_{\text{ben}} = (50.71)(0.4855) = 24.62\,\text{mm Hg}\), \(p_{\text{tol}} = (32.06)(0.5145) = 16.50\,\text{mm Hg}\), so \(p_{\text{total}} = 41.11\,\text{mm Hg}\).
Dalton's law for the vapour: \(y_{\text{ben}} = \frac{p_{\text{ben}}}{p_{\text{total}}} = \frac{24.62}{41.11} = 0.599\).
Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour phase \(= 0.599\) (and \(y_{\text{tol}} = 0.401\)). It exceeds the liquid-phase value of \(0.486\), the vapour being enriched in the more volatile benzene.
